Foretelling vs. Forthtelling
for-TEL-ing vurs forth-TEL-ing
noun phrase (two senses of prophecy)
From “foretell” (to predict) and “forthtell” (to declare forth); the distinction between prophecy as prediction of the future and prophecy as the bold declaration of God's word.

Biblical Definition

“Foretelling versus forthtelling” names the distinction between the two senses in which Scripture uses prophecy: foretelling, the prediction of things to come, and forthtelling, the bold declaration of the word of God to the present generation. The prophets did both. They foretold—the LORD does nothing but He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets—and the predictive element, fulfilled to the letter, is a chief proof of divine inspiration, for God alone declares the end from the beginning. But far more of their ministry was forthtelling: declaring the word God put in their mouths, calling the people to repentance, denouncing sin, comforting the afflicted, and pressing the claims of the covenant. The New Testament gift of prophecy is largely forthtelling in this sense—“he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.” The dictionary marks the distinction to correct two errors. The first reduces all prophecy to prediction, so that the prophet is treated as a mere fortune-teller and the prophetic books are mined only for end-times forecasts, missing their overwhelming burden of present-tense call and rebuke. The second, opposite error so emphasizes forthtelling that it denies genuine predictive prophecy altogether—the rationalist move that dates prophecies after the fact and strips Scripture of its supernatural foreknowledge. The dictionary holds both: God truly foretold the future, and His foretelling vindicates His Word; and God's prophets chiefly forthtold His will to their own age, as faithful preaching, grounded in the prophetic word, still does today.

Webster 1828 Definition

The distinction between prophecy as foretelling (prediction of the future) and forthtelling (bold declaration of God's word to the present); the prophets did both, and the dictionary affirms genuine prediction while recovering the larger burden of present-tense proclamation.

expand to see more

FORETELLING VS. FORTHTELLING, noun phrase. The two senses of biblical prophecy.

Foretelling: prediction of things to come, a proof of inspiration (Amos 3:7).

Forthtelling: the bold declaration of God's word to the present generation.

NT prophecy is largely forthtelling—edification, exhortation, comfort (1 Corinthians 14:3).

The prophets did both; both are grounded in the word God put in their mouths (Jeremiah 1:9).

Key Scripture

2 Pe 1:21 — "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

1 Co 14:3 — "But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort."

Am 3:7 — "Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets."

Jer 1:9 — "Then the LORD put forth his hand, and touched my mouth. And the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth."

Modern Corruption

One error reduces prophecy to mere prediction, treating prophets as fortune-tellers; the rationalist opposite denies genuine prediction, dating prophecies after the fact to strip Scripture of supernatural foreknowledge.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the full nature of biblical prophecy. One error reduces all prophecy to prediction, treating the prophets as fortune-tellers and the prophetic books as a quarry for end-times charts. This misses the overwhelming burden of their ministry, which was forthtelling—calling a covenant people to repentance, denouncing sin, comforting the afflicted, and pressing the word of God upon the present hour. The prophet was first a preacher, not a forecaster.

The opposite and graver error is the rationalist denial of genuine predictive prophecy. To escape the supernatural, critics date prophecies after the events they “predict”—Daniel to the second century, Isaiah's naming of Cyrus to a later hand. The dictionary rejects this: God truly foretold the future, declaring the end from the beginning, and the fulfilment of His predictions is a chief proof of inspiration, for He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets. The dictionary holds both senses together—real foretelling that vindicates the Word, and the larger forthtelling that faithful preaching, grounded in that Word, continues to this day.

Hebrew Roots

From “foretell” (to predict beforehand) and “forthtell” (to declare forth); both rendering the work of the Hebrew navi' (prophet, spokesman) and Greek prophetes.

expand to see more

“Foretell,” to predict the future, the predictive sense of prophecy.

“Forthtell,” to declare forth God's word to the present.

Navi', Hebrew, a prophet, a called spokesman for God.

Prophetes, Greek, one who speaks forth (pro- + phemi) the divine word.

Both grounded in the word God puts in the prophet's mouth (Jeremiah 1:9).

Usage

"The teacher distinguished foretelling from forthtelling to recover the prophets' burden of present-tense call."

"He defended genuine predictive prophecy against the rationalist dating of prophecies after the fact."

"She saw that faithful preaching today is forthtelling, grounded in the prophetic word."
